author: Victoria Law
title: Across the US, Incarcerated People Report Unsafe Meals — and It’s Getting Worse
content:
Stella longs for vegetables, sauce, and meat. She dreams of waffles with fresh strawberries, beef bacon and sausage links, and any type of Italian food.




But none of these are ever on the menu. Stella has been incarcerated in a Pennsylvania prison since the 1990s. “I always went to the dining room because the food was good, freshly made, and filling,” she recalled of that first decade in prison. “The menus were created by the supervisors and the inmates who worked there could cook food the way we wanted to.” (Stella, like nearly all of the incarcerated people interviewed for this report, asked that her full legal name not be published to avoid reprisals.)




In 2018, Aramark won the 

contract for food procurement in Pennsylvania’s prisons

. While the contract allowed the prisons to continue controlling staffing, meal service, and menus, Stella traces the decline in meals to that change.




Now, she told 

Truthout

, the meals are “disgusting, soy-based filler food. I live off of commissary and my health suffers because of it.”




Catherine entered prison the year that Aramark took over. “The food was more edible when I arrived,” she said. “There was more variety, especially with vegetables.”

title: Federal Government Is Targeting Officials Who Are Trying to Hold ICE Accountable
content:

.




In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.




In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the 

House Judiciary

 

Committee

 and the 

Department of Justice

 (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.

title: Incarcerated Los Angeles Youth Fought for the Right to Hug Their Parents — and Won
content:
This story was co-published with

 

Truthout

.




Mercedes Maradiaga sat across from her 19-year-old son in the Los Padrinos Juvenile Hall in Los Angeles in complete devastation. Her son had at that point been incarcerated at the prison for two years and she had visited him every weekend. But that day in September 2024 was especially hard because it was their first visit since he had been beaten by officers earlier that week in a space in the jail where there were no cameras. The guards had jumped on and kicked him, and he needed surgery for a torn ACL. All she wanted was to give him a hug and reassure him that she was there. However, because of the no-contact visit policies at Los Padrinos, she was unable to give him that comfort.




Even during birthdays and holidays, they weren’t allowed to embrace. The boy endured the jail’s horrible living conditions — including rat infestations and flooded toilets — but couldn’t hug his mom for a moment of escape.




“I couldn’t even let him know I’m here just with the little hug,” Maradiaga said. “It would have meant everything to him. It was sad, and I did that for four years.”
